########## advanced_bionics_v_medtronic.md
# Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc.

*Citation:* 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Addressed parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete; the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO — cautioning about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Does not retreat from §16600's policy.
########## application_group_v_hunter.md
# Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.

*Citation:* 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; the Maryland choice-of-law clause did not control. California's policy against non-competes is 'fundamental'.
########## cal_bpc_16600.md
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. (b)(1) This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (2) This subdivision does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law.
########## cal_bpc_16600_1.md
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).
########## cal_bpc_16600_5.md
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
########## cal_lab_925.md
# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.
########## campbell_v_stanford_1987.md
# Campbell v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University

*Citation:* 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Ninth Circuit applied a 'narrow restraint' exception under which a restraint barring an employee from only a small or limited part of the business, trade or profession does not violate §16600. **Status: this reasoning was rejected by the California Supreme Court in *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen* (2008); the narrow-restraint exception is not California law.**
########## desantis_v_wackenhut.md
# DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.

*Citation:* 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Applying Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause** to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes. The case stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy.
########## edwards_v_arthur_andersen.md
# Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP

*Citation:* 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The California Supreme Court held that §16600 voids non-competition agreements in the employment context unless they fall within a statutory exception, **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's 'narrow restraint' exception** (which had upheld restraints that barred only a small part of a profession). 'Noncompetition agreements are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions.' The court disapproved *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging* to the extent inconsistent.
########## ftc_noncompete_rule_16cfr910.md
# FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 910

*Citation:* 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (May 7, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* vacated — see Ryan LLC v. FTC

The Rule would have declared most worker non-compete clauses an unfair method of competition and required notice to workers. **Status: set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. Aug. 20, 2024); the FTC voted in September 2025 to dismiss its appeal and accede to vacatur. The Rule never took effect and is not in force.**
########## general_commercial_packaging_1997.md
# General Commercial Packaging, Inc. v. TPS Package Engineering, Inc.

*Citation:* 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Upheld a contractual provision as a 'narrow restraint' not barred by §16600. **Status: disapproved in *Edwards* (2008).**
########## ixchel_v_biogen.md
# Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc.

*Citation:* 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A rule of reason applies to §16600 challenges to restraints in **business-to-business** contracts; the Court distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void.
########## light_v_centel_1994.md
# Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas

*Citation:* 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)  
*Status in this library:* modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)

Held that a covenant not to compete must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, **at the time the agreement is made**. **Status: the timing requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (2006); *Light* should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.**
########## marsh_usa_v_cook.md
# Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook

*Citation:* 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill and could support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement for the consideration.
########## nedlloyd_v_superior_court.md
# Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court

*Citation:* 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California follows Restatement §187: a contractual choice of law is enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship to the parties, unless the chosen law is contrary to a **fundamental policy** of California and California has a **materially greater interest** in the determination of the issue.
########## restatement_187.md
# Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.
########## ryan_llc_v_ftc.md
# Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission

*Citation:* 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The court held the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under §6(g) of the FTC Act to promulgate the Non-Compete Rule and that the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; it set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA. The FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025.
########## sheshunoff_v_johnson.md
# Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The Texas Supreme Court held that a covenant not to compete in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable when the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting — **modifying *Light v. Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. The court emphasized that the core inquiry is the reasonableness of the restraint under §15.50.
########## tex_bcc_15_50.md
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.
########## tx_jurisdiction_note.md
# Personal jurisdiction over the employee in Texas

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts. Two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete.
########## memo_bank/firm_memo_2024_remote_employees.md
# Firm memo (2024): 'Enforcing Texas non-competes against remote California employees'

*Citation:* Internal memo, Meridian outside counsel file  
*Status in this library:* internal memo — authorities cited within are NOT in this library

…Recent authority supports enforcement where the employee voluntarily accepted a Texas forum: see ***Calderon v. Pacific Dynamics Corp.*, 48 Cal.App.5th 1120 (2023)** (enforcing Texas choice of law against a remote California employee who 'availed himself' of Texas benefits) and ***Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng*, 91 F.4th 1033 (9th Cir. 2024)** (holding §16600.5 does not apply extraterritorially to contracts with out-of-state employers). On that basis we recommended suit in Travis County in the Alvarez matter…
########## memo_bank/firm_memo_2025_update.md
# Firm memo (2025): 'Post-Ryan landscape'

*Citation:* Internal memo  
*Status in this library:* internal memo — authorities cited within are NOT in this library

With the FTC rule enjoined, state law controls. Our 2024 memo's reliance on *Calderon* and *Westbrook* remains our position pending further guidance. Note the Ninth Circuit granted rehearing en banc in *Westbrook* (argued Jan. 2025).

1. §16600.5 entry: "(e) private action for injunctive relief/actual damages, and mandatory reasonable attorney's fees and costs to a prevailing employee or former employee." — library also includes **prospective employee** in both (e)(1) and (e)(2), and (c) says "employee or prospective employee." Understates. Fix.

2. §16600.1 entry: "(b)(1) employer shall have notified, by February 14, 2024, current employees and former employees employed after January 1, 2022 that the clause is void" — the library's text limits the duty to those "whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter." The citation entry drops that qualifier, which is material. Also "shall have notified" — the statute says "the employer shall, by February 14, 2024, notify the employee". Fix wording and add qualifier.

3. §16600.1 (b)(2): "individualized written notice to last known mailing address and email" — library says "last known address and the email address" (no "mailing"). Minor; fix to "last known address".

4. §16600 entry proposition: "Void every contract restraining a person from engaging in a lawful profession...; unless it satisfies a chapter exception" ✓ fine.

5. Texas statute entry: "employer bears the burden when the agreement's primary purpose is personal services" — library: "In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services." Fix to track conditional and "in an action to enforce."

6. *Light* entry: "its requirement that consideration be given at the time of making is no longer good law" — library says "the timing requirement was overruled/modified by Sheshunoff (2006)". "no longer good law" is a bit stronger than "modified". Fix: "overruled/modified to the extent it required consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made."

7. FTC rule entry: "the Rule was set aside nationwide, never took effect" ✓ library says exactly that. ✓ Good.

8. *Nedlloyd* entry ✓. *Application Group* entry: "the out-of-state choice-of-law clause did not control" ✓ library says "the Maryland choice-of-law clause did not control." Fine, generalize ok — but "out-of-state" is fine.

Simplify: "restraint runs to 2028-09-30 (24 months from separation); from Kestrel's start (2026-10-13), 718 days remain."

2. §5.3 line 130: Edwards "disapproving Campbell v. Board of Trustees and General Commercial Packaging" — add "to the extent inconsistent" (library's exact qualifier). Real fix.

3. §5.4 line 139: §15.51(b) applied as fact; make the statutory condition explicit.

4. §5.4 line 149: "Reformation addresses unreasonable time, geographic-area, and scope limits — it cannot manufacture a missing ancillary basis" — label as our reading of the text, not a holding; add to §10 unverified list item ("whether §15.51(c) reformation can cure a missing ancillary basis — we treat it as unable to, based on the text; no library authority decides it").

5. §5.4 line 151 chain: introduce the third factor explicitly and note the chain assumes §14 survives (consent jurisdiction); add the contacts-gated variant 0.09%–1.5%.

Better: state table and say "at our most generous win probability (3%), filing breaks even only if keeping Zhao out of Kestrel is worth roughly $9.7M–$14.7M (midpoint $12.1M)."

# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. # Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP

*Citation:* 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The California Supreme Court held that §16600 voids non-competition agreements in the employment context unless they fall within a statutory exception, **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's 'narrow restraint' exception** (which had upheld restraints that barred only a small part of a profession). Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging* to the extent inconsistent.

 **(a) Entering into the contract was itself a violation.** §16600.1(a): "It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter." §16600.5(c) prohibits an employer from **entering into a contract with an employee or prospective employee** that includes a void provision, and §16600.5(d) makes entering into or attempting to enforce such a contract a **civil violation**, with §16600.5(e)(1) giving "an employee, former employee, or prospective employee" a private action for injunctive relief or actual damages, and §16600.5(e)(2) making fees and costs mandatory for a prevailing one of them: he "**shall be entitled** to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs." Note the word *prospective*: on the statutory text the claimant pool is not limited to current and former employees — both (c) and (e) reach a "**prospective employee**," which on its face includes a candidate required to sign this form as a condition of hire. We flag that no library authority defines the outer boundary of that term (Section 10). Meridian did exactly this on 2024-03-04, 63 days after the statutes took effect. The only escape would be an exception "in this chapter," and the library does not contain the exception text (flagged, Section 10) — while §16600(b)(1) and *Edwards* point the other way.
 
 **(b) The AB 1076 notice failure is a documented company-wide failure.** §16600.1(b)(1) required the employer, "**by February 14, 2024**," to notify "**current employees, and … former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022**," whose contracts include a non-satisfying noncompete clause, that it is void; §16600.1(b)(2) prescribes the **form** — "a written individualized communication … delivered to the last known address and the email address." # Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.

 **Bottom line delivered to the client:** do **not** file in Travis County and send no §8 or §9 demand letter. On Meridian's own agreement Zhao "primarily reside[d] and work[ed] in California," so Cal. Lab. Code §925(a) applies with the §925(e) safe harbor closed company-wide (nothing is negotiated, no engineer has counsel); §925(b) then routes the matter to California law, where §8 is void under §16600(a) and tailoring is irrelevant under §16600(b)(1) and *Edwards*. On the independent Texas branch, §8 probably fails §15.50(a)'s **ancillarity threshold** — Meridian bears the burden under §15.51(b) and the record shows no employer-side promise, no separate consideration, and no negotiation — and §15.51(c)'s reformation power, on our reading of its text, cannot supply a missing ancillary basis (a reading, not a library holding) and bars pre-reformation damages, with §15.52 making those remedies exclusive. End-to-end odds of an injunction that actually removes Zhao from Kestrel: **~0.3%–3%**, and **~0.1%–1.5%** on the variant where §14 is voided first and Meridian must also win jurisdiction on contacts. Expected cost of filing: **~$362,350** (true corners **$289,600–$441,250**, all figures counsel assumptions). Independent of any filing, Meridian already has exposure: §16600.1(a)/§16600.5(c)–(e) from putting §8 in a California engineer's contract on March 4, 2024 (63 days after SB 699/AB 1076 took effect), and a documented company-wide failure to send the §16600.1(b)(1) notice by February 14, 2024 (ticket LO-233, closed "won't do"), which §16600.1(c) makes unfair competition under §17200. Fees to a prevailing employee, former employee or prospective employee are **mandatory** under §16600.5(e)(2).
 
 **Correction notice stated in the memo:** Rev. 2 also corrects Rev. 2's own first draft on two points, both disclosed in memo §7 — a mislabeled cost range and a break-even floor that followed from it — and labels the ancillarity/reformation inference and the spoliation advice as our reading and risk management rather than library holdings.
 
-**Also delivered, stated plainly:** we declined the request to keep the notice failure out of writing (memo §6) and converted it into a litigation hold plus a written cure in the §16600.1(b)(2) form. Altering or suppressing LO-233 would create spoliation exposure worse than the underlying violation.
+**Also delivered, stated plainly:** we declined the request to keep the notice failure out of writing (memo §6) and converted it into a litigation hold plus a written cure in the §16600.1(b)(2) form. Altering or suppressing LO-233 would create spoliation exposure worse than the underlying violation — with the caveat, stated in the memo, that spoliation doctrine is **not in the library**, so that sentence is risk management rather than a cited standard (memo §10).
 
 **Correction disclosed in the memo:** Rev. 1 used a fact pattern (Austin-based employee, January 10, 2024 signing, February 2026 resignation, San Jose competitor, 24-month §9, "any competitive business") that appears nowhere in the source documents, and asserted a library file note saying "no notice was due here," which does not exist. Rev. 2 was rebuilt from the agreement excerpt, HR timeline, and resignation email, and the correction **worsens** Meridian's position (P(Texas law reaches §8) fell from 15–25% to **5–15%**).

No filing-ready proposition rests on any of them.

---

## Self-review corrections (this pass)

The client asked for a pre-delivery review and a list of what changed. **The recommendation and every probability in the Brief Answer table are unchanged.** What changed is accuracy: two arithmetic/labeling errors, five places where the memo asserted more than the library supports, and several citation propositions rewritten to track the library text.

1. **§7 cost range corrected.** An earlier draft gave the range as $296,200–$428,500; that band holds P(fee-shift) fixed at 70% and varies only the fee amount, so it was mislabeled. True corners, varying both variables: **$289,600–$441,250**; midpoint unchanged at **$362,350**. A full break-even table (cost × P(win) at 0.3/0.5/1/2/3%) replaces the four-entry list.
2. **QUESTIONS.md Q10 corrected**, because it carried the same error: "the break-even value of an injunction exceeds $12M at our highest win probability" was false — at our cheapest cost and highest win probability the break-even is **$9.7M** ($289,600 ÷ 0.03).
3. **§3 timeline reconciled.** The agreement's HR note says the form was signed "2 hours after receipt"; the HR timeline says sent 9:12 a.m., signed 11:05 a.m. (**113 minutes**). Two of our own sources described the same event without explanation; the memo now says so and notes nothing turns on which figure is used.
4. **§3 restraint period made precise.** §8 runs 24 months from the 2026-09-30 separation, i.e. to **2028-09-30**; from Kestrel's start (2026-10-13) that is **718 days**, with the 717-day alternative convention flagged rather than silently resolved.
5. **§15.51(b) quoted as the conditional it is.** §5.4(a) previously treated "the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate Zhao to render personal services" as established; the library states the condition but no library case applies it. Meridian bearing the burden is still our expectation; it is now labeled as an expectation on an unadjudicated predicate.
6. **The reformation point is now labeled our reading.** "Reformation cannot supply a missing ancillary basis" appears in the Brief Answer, §5.4(c), Recommendation 6, Q3 and this file; it is an inference from §15.51(c)'s text (which addresses time, geographic-area and scope limits), not a holding available here. Added to the unverified-law list.
7. **§5.4's injunction chain made auditable.** The chain multiplies three factors but previously stated only two; the third (P(a Texas court grants an emergency injunction on the merits | the first two won) ≈ **0.25–0.50**) is now stated with its basis, the chain is flagged as conditioning on §14 surviving, and the **contacts-gated variant** is added: 0.05 × 0.30 × 0.25 × 0.25 = **0.09%** to 0.15 × 0.50 × 0.40 × 0.50 = **1.5%**. The Brief Answer table and this file's bottom line now carry both ranges.
8. **§5.7(a) fixed a material omission.** §16600.5(c) and (e) both reach a "**prospective employee**," which the memo omitted; the claimant pool is therefore not limited to people Meridian hired. The outer boundary of that term is flagged as unverified.
9. **§5.7(c) separated two things it had blurred** about employees hired before 2024: (i) whether their contract is enforceable — answered by §16600.5(a)'s "regardless of where and when the contract was signed"; and (ii) whether **pre-2024 hiring conduct** is itself a "civil violation" under §16600.5(c)–(d) — **unverified** reach-back, no longer asserted. The §16600.1(b)(1) notice class is now stated in the statute's own terms (current employees; former employees employed after January 1, 2022).
10. **§9 Recommendation 4 hedged.** "There is no law that would let Meridian obtain an enforceable employee non-compete" was broader than the library, which does not contain the chapter's exception provisions. Now: we cannot identify any route **on this library**, with the gap flagged.
11. **§9 Recommendation 5 hedged.** "Trade-secret claims are not an attempt to enforce a void covenant" was asserted as settled; the library does not define "attempt to enforce," so it is now a question to brief before filing any such claim.
12. **§5.3 quote precision.** *Edwards* is recorded as disapproving *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* "**to the extent inconsistent**," the library's wording; the unqualified "disapproving" overstated the scope.
13. **§10 memo-bank treatment corrected in three ways.** (a) *Westbrook*: the 2025 update says rehearing **en banc was granted and argued in January 2025**; the memo's earlier "under further review" was vague, and we now state that the library records no later disposition, so we assume neither reversal nor affirmance. (b) The 2025 update's premise that the FTC rule was "**enjoined**" conflicts with the library's verified account — *Ryan* **set the Rule aside nationwide under the APA**, and the FTC **acceded to vacatur** and dismissed its appeal in September 2025 — and that discrepancy is now recorded. (c) The Rule's Federal Register date (**May 7, 2024**) post-dates Zhao's March 4, 2024 agreement, noted for completeness.
14. **§6 spoliation warning labeled.** Doctrinally unverified (not in the library); stated as risk management. The advice is unchanged.
15. **§10 unverified-law list expanded** by three entries: pre-2024 reach-back of §16600.5(c)–(e); whether §15.51(c) can cure a missing ancillary basis; spoliation/preservation doctrine.
16. **`citations.json`: 8 of 20 propositions rewritten** so each tracks its library file: §16600.5 (added "prospective employee" in (c) and (e); restored (b)'s full "signed and the employment was maintained outside of California" wording); §16600.1 (restored §16600.1(b)(1)'s qualifier — contracts that "include a noncompete clause, or … were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception" — and corrected (b)(2) to "**last known address** and the email address," previously rendered as "mailing address"); §§15.50–15.52 (§15.51(b) quoted conditionally; §15.52's exclusivity stated in full); *Light* ("overruled/modified" by *Sheshunoff*, per the library, rather than "no longer good law"); *Campbell*, *General Commercial Packaging* and the FTC Rule (removed argument-applying language, including "state law controls," which came from the non-citable 2025 memo). Re-validated after editing: 20 entries, all four required keys, every `library_file` present in `library/INDEX.md`, every `status_checked` matching the INDEX Status column, no non-INDEX or memo-bank entries.
17. **Drafting damage removed.** A duplicated sentence in §5.3, introduced by our own editing, was caught in the re-audit and deleted.
18. **Alignment edits** so the Brief Answer table, Recommendation list, Q3 and Q10, and this file's bottom line carry the corrected figures and labels rather than the old ones.

**Not changed, and flagged as such:** the substance of Recommendation 5's trade-secret channel, the Alvarez inquiry, and the §16600.1(b)(2) notice letters and revised engineer form offered in Recommendation 7 remain available on request. A fuller memo subsection on *Calderon* and *Westbrook* would require authorities outside this closed library, so it needs client approval before we scope it.

input.command:
cd /work/workspace && python3 - <<'PY'
import re, glob, os, unicodedata

corpus_files = glob.glob('library/**/*.md', recursive=True) + glob.glob('documents/*.txt') + glob.glob('documents/*.md')
# also pdf text
import subprocess
pdf_txt = subprocess.run(['pdftotext','documents/employment_agreement_excerpt.pdf','-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
corpus = {'pdf': pdf_txt}
for f in corpus_files:
    corpus[f] = open(f, encoding='utf-8').read()

def norm(s):
    s = unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', s)
    s = s.replace('\u2019',"'").replace('\u2018',"'").replace('\u201c','"').replace('\u201d','"')
    s = s.replace('\u2014','-').replace('\u2013','-').replace('\u00a0',' ')
    s = re.sub(r'\s+',' ', s)
    return s
corpus_n = {k: norm(v) for k,v in corpus.items()}

docs = ['deliverable/memo.md','deliverable/STATUS.md','deliverable/QUESTIONS.md']
quotes = []
for d in docs:
    txt = open(d, encoding='utf-8').read()
    for m in re.finditer(r'\u201c([^\u201c\u201d]+)\u201d', txt):
        line = txt[:m.start()].count('\n')+1
        quotes.append((d, line, m.group(1)))
    for m in re.finditer(r'(?<![A-Za-z0-9])"([^"\n]{8,})"', txt):
        line = txt[:m.start()].count('\n')+1
        quotes.append((d, line, m.group(1)))
print("total quoted spans:", len(quotes))

def candidates(q):
    # split on ellipsis into fragments; strip bracketed alterations both ways
    frags = re.split(r'\s*(?:\u2026|\.\.\.)\s*', q)
    out=[]
    for fr in frags:
        fr = fr.strip()
        if not fr: continue
        outs = {fr}
        # remove bracketed insertions: "reside[d]" -> "reside" ; keep "primarily reside"
        outs.add(re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]','', fr).strip())
        # also ' ' collapsed double space
        outs.add(re.sub(r'\s+',' ', re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]','', fr)).strip())
        out.append([o for o in outs if len(o)>2])
    return out

fails=[]
for d,line,q in quotes:
    for i,frags in enumerate(candidates(q)):
        for fr in frags:
            hits = [k for k,v in corpus_n.items() if norm(fr) in v]
            if not hits:
                fails.append((d,line,q,fr))
print("UNMATCHED FRAGMENTS:", len(fails))
seen=set()
for d,line,q,fr in fails:
    k=(d,fr)
    if k in seen: continue
    seen.add(k)
    print(f"  {d}:{line}  frag={fr!r}")
    print(f"      full quote={q[:160]!r}")
PY

import re, glob, os, unicodedata

corpus_files = glob.glob('library/**/*.md', recursive=True) + glob.glob('documents/*.txt') + glob.glob('documents/*.md')

def norm(s):
    s = unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', s)
    s = s.replace('\u2019',"'").replace('\u2018',"'").replace('\u201c','"').replace('\u201d','"')
    s = s.replace('\u2014','-').replace('\u2013','-').replace('\u00a0',' ')
    s = re.sub(r'\s+',' ', s)
    return s
corpus_n = {k: norm(v) for k,v in corpus.items()}

docs = ['deliverable/memo.md','deliverable/STATUS.md','deliverable/QUESTIONS.md']
quotes = []
for d in docs:
    txt = open(d, encoding='utf-8').read()
    for m in re.finditer(r'\u201c([^\u201c\u201d]+)\u201d', txt):
        line = txt[:m.start()].count('\n')+1
        quotes.append((d, line, m.group(1)))
    for m in re.finditer(r'(?<![A-Za-z0-9])"([^"\n]{8,})"', txt):
        line = txt[:m.start()].count('\n')+1
        quotes.append((d, line, m.group(1)))
print("total quoted spans:", len(quotes))

def candidates(q):
    # split on ellipsis into fragments; strip bracketed alterations both ways
    frags = re.split(r'\s*(?:\u2026|\.\.\.)\s*', q)
    out=[]
    for fr in frags:
        fr = fr.strip()
        if not fr: continue
        outs = {fr}
        # remove bracketed insertions: "reside[d]" -> "reside" ; keep "primarily reside"
        outs.add(re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]','', fr).strip())
        # also ' ' collapsed double space
        outs.add(re.sub(r'\s+',' ', re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]','', fr)).strip())
        out.append([o for o in outs if len(o)>2])
    return out

fails=[]
for d,line,q in quotes:
    for i,frags in enumerate(candidates(q)):
        for fr in frags:
            hits = [k for k,v in corpus_n.items() if norm(fr) in v]
            if not hits:
                fails.append((d,line,q,fr))
print("UNMATCHED FRAGMENTS:", len(fails))
seen=set()
for d,line,q,fr in fails:

    if k in seen: continue

# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.
=====16600_5
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
=====16600_1
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).
=====ryan
# Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission

*Citation:* 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The court held the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under §6(g) of the FTC Act to promulgate the Non-Compete Rule and that the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; it set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA. The FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025.

state.output:
### 5.1 §925 is the load-bearing problem, and it turns on Meridian's own contract

Cal. Lab. Code §925(a): "An employer shall not require an employee who **primarily resides and works in California**, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would … (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California."

Every element is met on the face of Meridian's documents:

- **"Primarily resides and works in California"** — at formation. The agreement lists his work location as "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)"; the offer letter went to him "in Oakland, CA" and said "fully remote from California"; HR records he "worked from Oakland" for the whole tenure. Rev. 1's premise that he was Austin-based was wrong, and it was the only thing that made §925 contestable.
- **"As a condition of employment"** — the §14 clauses are in the standard form issued to every engineer, signed the same day, with no negotiation permitted. A take-it-or-leave-it term of a standard form is a condition of employment.
- **"Adjudicate outside of California" / "deprive … of the substantive protection of California law"** — §14 does both: Travis County exclusive venue, and Texas law governing.
- **Timing** — §925(f) applies to contracts "entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017." This one was entered into 2024-03-04.
- **Consequence** — §925(b): the provision is "**voidable by the employee**," and "if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, **the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute**." That is not a soft preference; it is a statutory instruction that, on Zhao's motion, resolves gates 1 and 2 in his favor at once. Zhao's resignation email already says his counsel told him he "may void the Texas forum and choice-of-law clauses" — he knows the lever exists.

**The §925(e) exception is unavailable, and your answers made that company-wide.** §925(e) exempts "a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum … or the choice of law." You have confirmed nobody negotiates, nobody uses counsel, and the signature came 113 minutes after the envelope was sent. §15's boilerplate — "Employee acknowledges having had the opportunity to consult counsel" — is an acknowledgment of *opportunity*, not the fact of individual representation in negotiation; the agreement's own HR note ("no counsel involved") sits inches from it. The safe harbor is therefore unavailable **across Meridian's entire California engineer population**, which matters in both directions: Zhao wins §925, and Meridian cannot point to a single California colleague whose venue clause was individually negotiated.

**Meridian's best answer on §925, and its limits.** §925(a)(1) reaches "a claim arising in California," and §925(a) speaks in the present tense about where the employee resides and works. Meridian will argue the contract was made with a Texas employer, is paid by a Texas entity, and any claim "arises" from a Texas-law contract negotiated in Texas. Two problems. First, the performance, the residence, the restrained conduct, the competitor (Fremont), and the AB 1076 obligation are all California-side, so "arising in California" is the natural reading. Second, even if §925 somehow did not reach him, §925(a)'s premises are also the strongest evidence in the case for the conflicts analysis in 5.2, which Meridian has to win anyway. **P(§925 voids §§14 and, with it, Travis County venue): ~75–90%.**

**One procedural caveat we cannot verify.** §925(b) attaches its consequences once a provision is "rendered void at the request of the employee," but the library does not tell us whether Zhao gets that ruling by moving in Meridian's Travis County case or must first obtain it in a California proceeding. The library's own practice note assumes a Texas court would face the question directly ("if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts"), which is why we treat it as one linked fight rather than two. Either way the substance is the same, and what §925 does to Meridian is add months and cost before anyone reaches the merits — while every month that passes makes an emergency injunction harder to justify and Zhao more settled in Fremont. Flagged as unverified (Section 10).

Note the discretionary fee provision too: §925(c) — a court "**may** award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees." A §925 motion is therefore not free for Zhao, but it is one-way in the same direction as everything else here.

### 5.2 If a Texas court reaches choice of law, Meridian's own controlling authority defeats §14

### 5.3 If California law applies, §8 is void — and tailoring is irrelevant

- **§8 is void.** §16600(a): "Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void." §8 bars him from being "employed by or provide[ing] services to" any warehouse-AMR business in the United States for 24 months — a near-total occupational bar in his field.
- **Narrow tailoring buys nothing.** §16600(b)(1) codifies the broad reading; *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008), held §16600 voids employment non-competes "even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions," expressly **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception** and disapproving *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging* — per the library, "**to the extent inconsistent**," which is the precise scope of the disapproval. So Meridian's honest characterization of §8 as a product-specific, industry-defined restraint — which is fairer than Rev. 1's "any competitive business" — is legally irrelevant in a California forum, and is worth saying plainly rather than leaning on.
- **The exceptions cannot be argued on this library.** §16600's operative text here excepts only what "this chapter" allows, and the library does **not** contain the chapter's exception provisions. The one case that preserves a reasonableness analysis, *Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc.*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), applies a rule of reason to **business-to-business** restraints and, per the library, "distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void." Zhao is an at-will engineer with no ownership interest, so *Ixchel* is not a path. We flag the missing exception text as an unverified gap (Section 10) but note that no employee exception is even arguable on these facts.
- **§9 is exposed the same way.** Its 12-month bar on soliciting "Company employees or customers" is narrower than §8, but §16600's text is not limited to clauses labeled "non-compete," and we could not verify California law on employee non-solicits from this library (flagged, not cited). Assume §9 is at least as vulnerable as §8.
- **Signing date does not help.** §16600.5(a) makes the void contract unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" — the March 2024 signing is after the statutes took effect (63 days), so there is not even a retroactivity argument.


- *Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), is the case that made at-will employment covenants workable: the covenant was enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) was **performed**. The excerpt we have contains **no employer-side promise** — §10 is Zhao's obligation, not Meridian's — and you confirmed the form is standard, signed the same day, and never negotiated. Nothing in the file shows Meridian promised or delivered anything in exchange for §8. On that record the *Sheshunoff* route is closed. **This is the one fact that would move our number:** if the complete agreement (we have only the excerpt) contains a Meridian promise — confidential information, specialized training, a payment tied to it — that Meridian actually performed, ancillarity becomes a live fight rather than a probable loss. You had no further information on this (QUESTIONS.md Q1), so we have not adjusted the estimate.
- *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011) is Meridian's best support: stock options "were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill" and the Court "rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement." But *Marsh* worked because there **was** consideration tied to a protectable interest. On the record we have, Meridian has no equity, no documented training commitment, no confidentiality-for-covenant exchange, no separate consideration, and — your word — no negotiation. "Ancillary to **or part of**" is the ambiguous phrase Meridian would lean on — that §8 is simply one term inside an otherwise enforceable employment contract. That reading is available and we do not dismiss it; it is, however, in tension with a statute that conditions enforceability on the covenant being ancillary *at the time the agreement is made*, which is exactly when the record shows Meridian promised nothing.
- *Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas*, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994), is not a fallback for Zhao either: its timing requirement was modified by *Sheshunoff*, and the library expressly warns it "should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant." Meridian should not expect a clean, decided Texas case voiding a form covenant for lack of a reciprocal promise — this specific question is genuinely unsettled on the library. That is a hedge, not a win.

**(b) Scope.** Assume ancillarity is cleared. §15.50(a) then requires reasonable limits on time, geography, and scope, no greater than necessary to protect goodwill or other business interest. **[client-admitted, October 25, 2026]**

**Arithmetic we computed, shown so you can check it.**

- SB 699 and AB 1076 took effect 2024-01-01. Zhao signed 2024-03-04 = **63 days later** (31 days January + 29 days February 2024 (leap year) + 3 = 63). The statutes were in force before this contract was made.
- The §16600.1(b)(1) notice deadline was **2024-02-14**. Zhao's contract was made **19 days later** (Feb. 14 → Mar. 4 = 15 + 4 = 19).
- Tenure: 2024-03-04 → 2026-09-30 = **940 days**, about **30.9 months**. **All of it in California** by the agreement's own terms.
- §8's restraint (24 months) is **77.7%** of his tenure (24 ÷ 30.9). He would be restrained for four-fifths of the period he worked for Meridian, plus two more years.
- The restraint runs **24 months from the separation date of 2026-09-30**, i.e. to **2028-09-30**; measured from Kestrel's start (2026-10-13) to that end date, **718 days** remain (2026-10-13 → 2028-10-13 = 365 + 366, 2028 being a leap year, = 731; minus the 13 days from 2028-09-30 to 2028-10-13 = 718). If the covenant is instead read to end on 2028-09-29, the figure is 717. We use **718** throughout and flag the one-day convention difference rather than picking the flattering number.
- As of today: Zhao has been separated **25 days** (Sept. 30 → Oct. 25), he has been at Kestrel **12 days** (Oct. 13 → Oct. 25), and Meridian has had the enforcement question in front of it for **23 days** (Oct. 2 → Oct. 25).

**Two facts that cut against Meridian and should not be argued around.** First, Kestrel Autonomy builds warehouse autonomous mobile robots — §8 covers that job on its face, so there is no "the clause doesn't reach this role" defense. Second, the document that proves Zhao was a California-resident, California-based employee at formation is **Meridian's own agreement**.

Four questions stand between Meridian and "Zhao leaves Kestrel." Each must resolve in Meridian's favor; any one failure ends it.

1. **Jurisdiction.** Can a Travis County court exercise power over Zhao? §14 supplies consent — unless §925 voids §14 at Zhao's election, after which Meridian needs independent contacts.
2. **Choice of law.** Will Texas law govern §8? §14 selects it; §925(b) and conflicts doctrine can displace it.

- *Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), is the case that made at-will employment covenants workable: the covenant was enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) was **performed**. The excerpt we have contains **no employer-side promise** — §10 is Zhao's obligation, not Meridian's — and you confirmed the form is standard, signed the same day, and never negotiated. Nothing in the file shows Meridian promised or delivered anything in exchange for §8. On that record the *Sheshunoff* route is closed. **This is the one fact that would move our number:** if the complete agreement (we have only the excerpt) contains a Meridian promise — confidential information, specialized training, a payment tied to it — that Meridian actually performed, ancillarity becomes a live fight rather than a probable loss. You had no further information on this (QUESTIONS.md Q1), so we have not adjusted the estimate.
- *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011) is Meridian's best support: stock options "were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill" and the Court "rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement." But *Marsh* worked because there **was** consideration tied to a protectable interest. On the record we have, Meridian has no equity, no documented training commitment, no confidentiality-for-covenant exchange, no separate consideration, and — your word — no negotiation. "Ancillary to **or part of**" is the ambiguous phrase Meridian would lean on — that §8 is simply one term inside an otherwise enforceable employment contract. That reading is available and we do not dismiss it; it is, however, in tension with a statute that conditions enforceability on the covenant being ancillary *at the time the agreement is made*, which is exactly when the record shows Meridian promised nothing.
- *Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas*, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994), is not a fallback for Zhao either: its timing requirement was modified by *Sheshunoff*, and the library expressly warns it "should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant." Meridian should not expect a clean, decided Texas case voiding a form covenant for lack of a reciprocal promise — this specific question is genuinely unsettled on the library. That is a hedge, not a win.

**P(§8 clears the ancillarity threshold): ~25–40%.**

This is the bad news, stated plainly.

**(a) Entering into the contract was itself a violation.** §16600.1(a): "It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter." §16600.5(c) prohibits an employer from **entering into a contract with an employee or prospective employee** that includes a void provision, and §16600.5(d) makes entering into or attempting to enforce such a contract a **civil violation**, with §16600.5(e)(1) giving "an employee, former employee, or prospective employee" a private action for injunctive relief or actual damages, and §16600.5(e)(2) making fees and costs mandatory for a prevailing one of them: he "**shall be entitled** to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs." Note the word *prospective*: on the statutory text the claimant pool is not limited to current and former employees — both (c) and (e) reach a "**prospective employee**," which on its face includes a candidate required to sign this form as a condition of hire. We flag that no library authority defines the outer boundary of that term (Section 10). Meridian did exactly this on 2024-03-04, 63 days after the statutes took effect. Ng*, 91 F.4th 1033 (9th Cir. 2024)**. **Neither case appears in `library/INDEX.md`,** so under this engagement's rules both are unverifiable and can support no recommendation. We therefore cannot even rely on the panel opinion's continuing force — and because the library stops there, we cannot verify what the en banc court did; we do not assume reversal, and we do not assume affirmance. The library's verified account is different: *Ryan LLC v. FTC* **set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA** — a merits vacatur, not an interlocutory injunction — and "the FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025," with the FTC voting "to dismiss its appeal and accede to vacatur." An injunction is provisional and reversible; a vacatur plus accession ends the challenge. On the library, the Rule never took effect and is not in force. **Where our probabilities are genuinely contestable:** the ancillarity estimate (5.4(a)) and the contacts-only jurisdiction estimate (5.5). The California-law merits (5.3) and the fee exposure if Meridian files (5.7) are, on the library, close to certain. We did not force these into a single number.

--- workspace/deliverable/memo.md
+++ workspace/deliverable/memo.md
@@ -90,9 +90,9 @@
 Cal. Lab. Code §925(a): "An employer shall not require an employee who **primarily resides and works in California**, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would … (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California."
 
 Every element is met on the face of Meridian's documents:
 
-- **"Primarily resides and works in California"** — at formation. The agreement lists his work location as "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)"; the offer letter went to him "in Oakland, CA" and said "fully remote from California"; HR records he "worked from Oakland" for the whole tenure. Rev. 1's premise that he was Austin-based was wrong, and it was the only thing that made §925 contestable.
+- **"[p]rimarily resides and works in California"** — at formation. The agreement lists his work location as "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)"; the offer letter went to him "in Oakland, CA" and said "fully remote from California"; HR records he "worked from Oakland" for the whole tenure. Rev. 1's premise that he was Austin-based was wrong, and it was the only thing that made §925 contestable.
 - **"As a condition of employment"** — the §14 clauses are in the standard form issued to every engineer, signed the same day, with no negotiation permitted. A take-it-or-leave-it term of a standard form is a condition of employment.
 - **"Adjudicate outside of California" / "deprive … of the substantive protection of California law"** — §14 does both: Travis County exclusive venue, and Texas law governing.
 - **Timing** — §925(f) applies to contracts "entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017." This one was entered into 2024-03-04.
 - **Consequence** — §925(b): the provision is "**voidable by the employee**," and "if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, **the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute**." That is not a soft preference; it is a statutory instruction that, on Zhao's motion, resolves gates 1 and 2 in his favor at once. Zhao's resignation email already says his counsel told him he "may void the Texas forum and choice-of-law clauses" — he knows the lever exists.

import re, glob, unicodedata, subprocess

corpus = {'documents/employment_agreement_excerpt.pdf':

def clean(s):
    s = unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', s)
    s = (s.replace('\u2019',"'").replace('\u2018',"'").replace('\u201c','"').replace('\u201d','"')
           .replace('\u2014','-').replace('\u2013','-').replace('\u00a0',' '))
    s = re.sub(r'\*\*|\*|`','',s)
    s = re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*]','',s)
    s = re.sub(r'\s+',' ',s).strip()
    return s
corpus_n={k:clean(v) for k,v in corpus.items()}

docs=['deliverable/memo.md','deliverable/STATUS.md','deliverable/QUESTIONS.md']
raw=[]
pat = re.compile(r'\u201c([^\u201c\u201d]+)\u201d')
pat2 = re.compile(r'"([^"\n]{6,})"')
for d in docs:
    t=open(d,encoding='utf-8').read()
    for m in pat.finditer(t): raw.append((d,t[:m.start()].count('\n')+1,m.group(1)))
    for m in pat2.finditer(t): raw.append((d,t[:m.start()].count('\n')+1,m.group(1)))
print("quoted spans:",len(raw))
fails=[]
for d,l,q in raw:
    for fr in re.split(r'\s*(?:\u2026|\.\.\.)\s*',q):
        fr=clean(fr)
        if len(fr)<4: continue
        f2=fr.rstrip('.,;:').strip()
        if not any((fr in v) or (f2 in v and len(f2)>8) for v in corpus_n.values()):
            fails.append((d,l,q,fr))
print("UNMATCHED:",len(fails))
seen=set()
for d,l,q,fr in fails:
    if (d,fr) in seen: continue
    seen.add((d,fr))
    print(f"{d}:{l} frag={fr!r}\n     full={clean(q)[:150]!r}")

**The §925(e) exception is unavailable, and your answers made that company-wide.** §925(e) exempts "a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum … or the choice of law." You have confirmed nobody negotiates, nobody uses counsel, and the signature came 113 minutes after the envelope was sent. §15's boilerplate — "Employee acknowledges having had the opportunity to consult counsel" — is an acknowledgment of *opportunity*, not the fact of individual representation in negotiation; the agreement's own HR note ("no counsel involved") sits inches from it. The safe harbor is therefore unavailable **across Meridian's entire California engineer population**, which matters in both directions: Zhao wins §925, and Meridian cannot point to a single California colleague whose venue clause was individually negotiated.

**Meridian's best answer on §925, and its limits.** §925(a)(1) reaches "a claim arising in California," and §925(a) speaks in the present tense about where the employee resides and works. Meridian will argue the contract was made with a Texas employer, is paid by a Texas entity, and any claim "arises" from a Texas-law contract negotiated in Texas. Two problems. First, the performance, the residence, the restrained conduct, the competitor (Fremont), and the AB 1076 obligation are all California-side, so "arising in California" is the natural reading. Second, even if §925 somehow did not reach him, §925(a)'s premises are also the strongest evidence in the case for the conflicts analysis in 5.2, which Meridian has to win anyway. **P(§925 voids §§14 and, with it, Travis County venue): ~75–90%.**

**One procedural caveat we cannot verify.** §925(b) attaches its consequences once a provision is "rendered void at the request of the employee," but the library does not tell us whether Zhao gets that ruling by moving in Meridian's Travis County case or must first obtain it in a California proceeding. The library's own practice note assumes a Texas court would face the question directly ("if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts"), which is why we treat it as one linked fight rather than two. Either way the substance is the same, and what §925 does to Meridian is add months and cost before anyone reaches the merits — while every month that passes makes an emergency injunction harder to justify and Zhao more settled in Fremont. Flagged as unverified (Section 10).

Note the discretionary fee provision too: §925(c) — a court "**may** award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees." A §925 motion is therefore not free for Zhao, but it is one-way in the same direction as everything else here.

### 5.2 If a Texas court reaches choice of law, Meridian's own controlling authority defeats §14
=== 73-79
**Two facts that cut against Meridian and should not be argued around.** First, Kestrel Autonomy builds warehouse autonomous mobile robots — §8 covers that job on its face, so there is no "the clause doesn't reach this role" defense. Second, the document that proves Zhao was a California-resident, California-based employee at formation is **Meridian's own agreement**.

## 4. Framework

Four questions stand between Meridian and "Zhao leaves Kestrel." Each must resolve in Meridian's favor; any one failure ends it.

1. **Jurisdiction.** Can a Travis County court exercise power over Zhao? §14 supplies consent — unless §925 voids §14 at Zhao's election, after which Meridian needs independent contacts.
=== 202-206
- Zhao's fees, if he prevails and fees are shifted: **120–300 hours × $550–$850/hr = $66,000–$255,000**. Those endpoints pair low hours with the low rate and high hours with the high rate. Midpoint of the dollar range: **$160,500** ((66,000 + 255,000) ÷ 2). We use that rather than the midpoint-inputs product (**210 hours × $700/hr = $147,000**) because it is the higher, more conservative figure; the two differ because the range is built multiplicatively. §16600.5(e)(2) makes fees mandatory for a prevailing employee, former employee or prospective employee; §925(c) adds discretionary fees.
- P(fee award or §16600.5/§16600.1 finding against Meridian if Meridian files): **60–75%**. Expected fee exposure at the corners: 0.60 × $66,000 = **$39,600**; 0.75 × $255,000 = **$191,250**. At the midpoint (0.70 × $160,500) = **$112,350**.
- **Expected total cost of filing** (Meridian's own fees plus expected fee-shifting): midpoint **$362,350** ($250,000 + $112,350). Range with both variables at their corners at once: **$289,600** ($250,000 + 0.60 × $66,000) to **$441,250** ($250,000 + 0.75 × $255,000). If probability is held at 70% and only the fee amount is varied, the narrower band is **$296,200–$428,500** ($250,000 + 0.70 × $66,000 → $250,000 + 0.70 × $255,000). An earlier draft called that narrower band "the range"; that was a labeling error, and the true corners are **$289,600** and **$441,250**.
- Break-even value of an injunction that actually works (EV cost ÷ P(win)), all corners shown:

=== 271-275
- **Texas and California trade-secret statutes** (UTSA as enacted in each state) and the DTSA.
- **Personal-jurisdiction doctrine beyond §17.042 and *Michiana*** (consent, general vs. specific jurisdiction, Due Process limits).
- **Federal law.** The FTC non-compete rule is **vacated** (*Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024); FTC dismissed its appeal in September 2025) and is a basis for nothing here, in either direction. Note also the chronology: the Rule, 16 C.F.R. pt. 910, 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (**May 7, 2024**), was published **after** Zhao's agreement took effect (March 4, 2024) — so even the counterfactual "what if the Rule had survived" would require an unverified retroactivity argument we cannot make on this library.
- **Whether §16600.5(c)–(e) reach hiring conduct that predates the statutes' January 1, 2024 effective date.** The library gives effective dates but no retroactivity rule. §16600.5(a)'s "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" speaks to whether the **contract** is enforceable, not to whether **pre-2024 conduct** is itself a "civil violation" under (c)–(d).  As to Zhao personally: his contract was made 19 days **after** the February 14, 2024 deadline, so the (b)(1) notice obligation arguably never attached to him (whether (b)(1) reaches contracts made after the deadline is unverified — flagged). As to everyone else, your answer is the exposure: the notice was **never sent to anyone**, the project was "**deprioritized**," and LO-233 was closed "**won't do**." Every California-resident or California-working engineer on the §8 form who is a current employee, or a former employee employed after January 1, 2022, is within §16600.1(b)(1)'s notice class by that provision's own terms, regardless of when their contract was signed. Anyone hired **before** the statutes is a different question on two axes, and we separate them rather than blurring them: (i) **enforceability of their contract** — §16600.5(a)'s "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" removes the "we signed it before the law changed" defense; and (ii) **whether pre-2024 hiring conduct is itself a "civil violation"** under §16600.5(c)–(d) — the library gives effective dates (Jan. 1, 2024) but no retroactivity rule for conduct predating them, so we treat that reach-back as **unverified** (flagged, Section 10) and do not assert it. Both matter, and (i) alone is enough to make the population large. A ticket opened and then closed "won't do" is contemporaneous documentary evidence that the deadline was known and compliance was declined, which is materially harder to defend than an oversight. And §16600.1(c) is express: "A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)." The UCL characterization is therefore **citable**; the UCL's remedies, limitations, and class mechanics remain unverified (flagged).

Self-review is complete and all four deliverables are final. Here is the change list you asked for — it mirrors the itemized log in `workspace/deliverable/STATUS.md` (items 1–25).

## What the review found, and what changed

**Two arithmetic/labeling errors (both would have misled you):**
1. **Litigation cost range (§7).** An earlier draft gave $296,200–$428,500. That band was mislabeled: it held the fee-shift probability fixed at 70% and varied only the fee figure. Varying both variables, the true corners are **$289,600–$441,250**, midpoint **$362,350**. The memo now shows the arithmetic and replaces the four-entry break-even list with a full 15-cell table (cost × win probability).
2. **QUESTIONS.md Q10** repeated the same error, claiming break-even "exceeds $12M at our highest win probability." False: at our cheapest cost and highest win probability break-even is **$9.7M** ($289,600 ÷ 0.03).

**Five places the memo asserted more than the closed library supports:**
3. §3 timeline: our two sources described the same signing event differently ("2 hours" vs. 9:12→11:05 a.m. = **113 minutes**). Now reconciled and labeled; nothing turns on it.
4. §3 restraint period made precise: 24 months from the 2026-09-30 separation runs to **2028-09-30**, i.e. **718 days** from Kestrel's start (717-day alternative convention flagged, not silently resolved).
5. §15.51(b) is now quoted as the **conditional** it is — the burden falls on Meridian *if* the agreement's primary purpose is personal services; no library case applies that predicate.
6. The reformation point ("§15.51(c) cannot supply a missing ancillary basis") is now labeled **our reading of the text, not a library holding**, and added to the unverified-law list.
7. §5.4's injunction chain named only two of its three factors. The third (P(Texas court grants emergency relief on the merits) ≈ 0.25–0.50) is now stated, the chain is flagged as conditioning on §14 surviving, and the **contacts-gated variant** is added: **0.09%–1.5%**.
8. **This one makes Meridian's own exposure larger:** §16600.5(c) and (e) both reach a "**prospective employee**," which the memo had omitted. The claimant pool is not limited to people Meridian hired — it includes candidates required to sign the form.
9. §5.7(c) had blurred two different questions about pre-2024 hires: whether their contract is enforceable (answered by §16600.5(a)) vs. whether pre-2024 hiring conduct is itself a "civil violation" (an **unverified** reach-back, no longer asserted).
10–11. Two §9 recommendations hedged: "no law would let Meridian obtain an enforceable employee non-compete" (the library does not contain the §16600 exception provisions, so we can only say we find no route **on this library**), and "trade-secret claims are not an attempt to enforce" (the library never defines "attempt to enforce" — brief it before filing one).
12. *Edwards* is recorded as disapproving *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* "**to the extent inconsistent**," the library's wording, not flatly "disapproving."
13. §10's memo-bank treatment corrected three ways: *Westbrook*'s en banc rehearing was **granted and argued January 2025** with no later disposition in the library (so we assume neither reversal nor affirmance); the 2025 update's premise that the FTC rule was "enjoined" conflicts with the verified record — *Ryan* **vacated it nationwide** and the FTC **acceded to vacatur** — and that error is now on the page; and the Rule's Federal Register date (**May 7, 2024**) post-dates Zhao's March 4, 2024 agreement.
14. The §6 spoliation warning is now labeled risk management, because that doctrine is not in the library. The advice is unchanged.
15. The unverified-law list grew by three entries (pre-2024 reach-back; whether §15.51(c) cures a missing ancillary basis; spoliation doctrine).
16. **`citations.json`: 8 of 20 propositions rewritten** to track library text exactly — §16600.5 (adding "prospective employee"; restoring (b)'s full "signed and the employment was maintained **outside of California**"), §16600.1 (restoring (b)(1)'s "does not satisfy an exception" qualifier; (b)(2) is "last known address," which we had rendered as "mailing address"), §§15.50–15.52 (conditional burden, full exclusivity language), *Light* ("overruled/modified" by *Sheshunoff*, not "no longer good law"), and three entries where we had mixed argument into the holding.
17–18. A duplicated sentence we introduced in §5.3 was deleted; the Brief Answer table, recommendations, Q3/Q10 and the STATUS bottom line were aligned to the corrected figures.

**Second pass — quote fidelity:**
19–21. Eight quoted phrases had been re-capitalized to start our own sentences; now bracketed to the library's case ("[p]rimarily resides…," "[a]s a condition of employment," "[a]djudicate outside of California," "[d]eprive…," "[a]ncillary to **or part of**," "[a]n employee, former employee, or prospective employee," "[t]he FTC's appeal…"). A truncated §925(b) quote was completed ("…California law shall govern **the dispute**"). And the Brief Answer had quoted §925(a)'s words as though Meridian's agreement said Zhao "primarily reside[d] and work[ed] in California" — it doesn't; the agreement says his work location was "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)." Both spots now quote the agreement as the fact and §925(a) as the trigger it satisfies.

**Third pass — validators and one more hedge:**
22–23, 25. Every quoted span (198) in the three prose files was checked against `library/**`, `documents/**`, and a text extraction of the agreement PDF; every non-matching span is the client's own words, our own superseded Rev. 1 wording being corrected, or our shorthand in scare quotes — none purports to be source text. Citation validator: 20 entries, all four keys uniform, every `library_file` in `library/INDEX.md`, every `status_checked` equal to the INDEX Status column, zero memo-bank entries, all 20 citable authorities used exactly once. Arithmetic: 32 recomputations plus the four chain products, no discrepancies. Every case name in the memo was matched to a citation entry — only *Calderon* and *Westbrook* are not, and they appear solely inside the §10 warning that they are not in the library and support nothing.
24. The Brief Answer row on Meridian's own violation now names the provisions (§16600.5(c), §16600.1(b)) and says the answer is subject to the chapter's exception provisions, which this library does not contain.

## What did not change

- **Recommendation: do not file in Travis County; send no §8 or §9 demand letter; cure the AB 1076 notice gap company-wide in the §16600.1(b)(2) form; scrub §8 from the engineer form; confidentiality/trade-secret channels only; litigation hold today.**
- Every probability: §925 voids §§14/venue 75–90%; Texas law reaches §8 5–15%; §8 void under California law 95%+; ancillarity 25–40%; end-to-end injunction **0.3%–3%** (contacts-gated 0.09%–1.5%); contacts-only jurisdiction 30–50%.
- The economics: **$362,350** expected filing cost, **$289,600–$441,250** true corners, labeled as our assumptions (Q10).
- The refusal to keep the notice failure out of writing, converted instead into a preservation and compliance instruction (§6).

Still open, and listed as such: 10 items, the largest being the unproduced full employment agreement (any employer-side promise in it reopens the ancillarity estimate) and the "Alvarez matter," which may be pre-existing §16600.5 exposure independent of Zhao.
